arXiv:2610.13113v1 [cs.LG] 09 Oct 2026

Continually Post-training Small Models
via Synthetic Self-distillation

Woosung Koh* Affiliation: KAIST AI    Hyunsoo Lee Affiliation: LG AI Research    Kyungjae Lee Affiliation: LG AI Research    Haeju Park Affiliation: LG AI Research    Dahyun Lee Affiliation: LG AI Research    Dasol Hwang Affiliation: LG AI Research    Moontae Lee Affiliation: LG AI Research    *Work done during an internship at LG AI Research Corresponding author
Abstract

Continual post-training faces a dual challenge of acquisition and retention: models must learn new capabilities while preserving prior knowledge. While Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) mitigates this using self-supervision with in-context demonstrations, it relies on strong in-context learning and instruction-following abilities. Consequently, SDFT fails on smaller models critical for low-latency, on-device use. To enable continual learning at smaller scales, we first identify the root cause of failure. We show that poor acquisition and forgetting correlate linearly with the post-trained model’s distribution shift, revealing the necessity of in-distribution learning. We thus introduce Synthetic Self-Distillation (SynthSelf), imitating SDFT’s in-distribution rewrite by outsourcing the task to a minimally larger, same-family aligner. Coupled with off-policy supervision and rejection sampling, this provides the high-quality supervision small models require without breaking their original distribution. Evaluations spanning 4 acquisition datasets (including a mixture) and 14 retention benchmarks show SynthSelf consistently outperforms 6 methods (including off- and on-policy distillation) across 3 small model scales. Extensive further analyses confirm SynthSelf paves the way toward effective small-model continual learning.

1 Introduction

Continual post-training of language models (LMs) is a common setting where practitioners aim to inject new capabilities into already-trained models for scenarios such as customizing for specific use-cases and enabling human-like lifelong learning (Shi et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024a; Zheng et al., 2025a; Zheng et al., 2025b; Srijith et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026a). Yet, this process is notoriously challenging on both the acquisition (injecting new abilities) and retention (maintaining existing capabilities) axes (Harmon et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026b). The failure to retain existing capabilities, widely known as catastrophic forgetting (McCloskey and Cohen, 1989; French, 1999; Kirkpatrick et al., 2017), is particularly well-documented in settings where a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) dataset is used for teacher forcing (Kalajdzievski, 2024; Luo et al., 2025; Lai et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b; Shenfeld et al., 2026b).

A recent work showed that self-distillation fine-tuning (SDFT) is an effective way to inject SFT demonstrations in an on-policy manner (Shenfeld et al., 2026a), outperforming recent off-policy continual fine-tuning methods such as re-invoke (Lu and Lab, 2025) and Dynamic Fine-tuning (DFT; Wu et al. (2026)) on both acquisition and retention axes. SDFT leverages the in-context learning (ICL) and instruction-following (IF) abilities of post-trained models to provide demonstrations in-context to the self-teacher model, and applies on-policy distillation (OPD; Ross et al. (2011), Agarwal et al. (2024)) on itself, supervising on an implicit self-rewrite of the demonstrations.

However, as models struggle with ICL and IF at smaller scales, SDFT remains infeasible in this regime (see Fig. 3(a)). We aim to address this limitation, as small models have become critical for applications such as on-device deployment, latency-specialized models, draft models, verifiers, and large-small collaborative methods (Cobbe et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2023; Abdin et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025; Belcak et al., 2025; Cai et al., 2026).

Contribution.

To better understand how to leverage the key principles of SDFT, we first examine why it succeeds in continual post-training (§ 2.2.1). We reveal that the distribution shift of the post-trained base model linearly correlates with poor acquisition and forgetting (Fig. 2), indicating that staying in-distribution is crucial for continual learning. While the primary advantage of SDFT over off-policy methods is its ability to staying in distribution, evaluating its self-generated offline dataset reveals that SDFT’s self-supervision quality is inadequate at smaller model scales (Fig. 3).

In response, we propose Synthetic Self-Distillation (SynthSelf), which imitates self-distillation’s implicit in-distribution rewrite by outsourcing the distribution-aligned rewrite to a larger model (§ 2.4). Our method distinctly differs from SDFT in the following ways: (i) choosing off-policy over on-policy supervision allows us to apply rejection sampling, which in turn improves supervision quality for small models that are sensitive to data quality; and (ii) using minimally larger, same-family aligners allows us to simultaneously (ii.a.) provide high-quality supervision (Tab. 2), (ii.b.) remain in-distribution relative to the base model (Fig. 5), and (ii.c.) maintain low computational costs. We empirically validate SynthSelf (§ 3), demonstrating that:

  1. 1.

    SynthSelf achieves the best acquisition across 3 domains (science, tool-use, and medicine) and a 4-subject science mixture while preserving prior capabilities on 14 benchmarks, consistently across 3 base model sizes (0.5, 1.5, 3B), and against 4 relevant baselines (Fig. 1, Tab. 1).

  2. 2.

    Controlling for the confounding factor of teacher model size, we demonstrate that SynthSelf outperforms both on- and off-policy distillation in acquisition by +5.7%p to +16.9%p, averaged over all four settings and three base scales (Tab. 1, Fig. 5).

  3. 3.

    We show that utilizing a smaller (weaker) in-distribution aligner is more effective than deploying a larger (stronger) out-of-distribution teacher, yielding a 69.9% reduction in alignment computational cost (FLOPs) (Tab. 2).

  4. 4.

    We validate that our improvement over SDFT is not due to prompt differences using prompt-matched and diverse prompts, achieving +18.96%p and +1.68%p gains in acquisition and retention over prompt-matched SDFT (Fig. 6).

  5. 5.

    Finally, our ablation studies confirm that combining rejection sampling with off-policy supervision is a meaningful component of our methodology (Fig. 5).

2 Method

2.1 Problem Setting: Continual Fine-tuning

Continual fine-tuning.

Given a post-trained policy π\pi, we continually inject new knowledge from a dataset 𝒟train={(xi,yi)}i=1N\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} by further training π\pi. In doing so, we aim to maximize (i) acquisition: performance on a same-domain test set 𝒟test\mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}, while maintaining (ii) retention: performance on existing capabilities, evaluated via 𝒟ret\mathcal{D}_{\text{ret}}.

Self-distillation fine-tuning.

Given a demonstration pair (x,y)(x,y) and an SDFT prompt PSDFTP^{\text{SDFT}} that places the demonstration in-context, SDFT trains the policy πθ\pi_{\theta} parameterized by θ\theta on-policy toward the frozen model’s self-rewrite of that demonstration,

ℒ(θ)=DKL(πθ(⋅∣x)∥π(⋅∣PSDFT(x,y)))=𝔼y′∼πθ(⋅∣x)[logπθ​(y′∣x)π⁡(y′∣PSDFT​(x,y))],\mathcal{L}(\theta)\;=\;D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\,\big\|\,\pi\!\left(\cdot\mid P^{\text{SDFT}}(x,y)\right)\big)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\left[\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid x)}{\pi\!\left(y^{\prime}\mid P^{\text{SDFT}}(x,y)\right)}\right], (1)

where y′y^{\prime} denotes a completion sampled from the current policy. This supervision preserves the semantic content of yy while remaining within the model’s native distribution, allowing for effective continual learning.

2.2 In-distribution Demonstration Injection

2.2.1 In-distribution learning is key for continual learning

Building on the observation that SDFT preserves the native distribution, we hypothesize that training on out-of-distribution (OOD) targets is the primary driver of poor acquisition and forgetting. To test this, we continually fine-tune Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (Qwen et al., 2025), measuring the resulting policy shift via DKL(πafter∥πbefore)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\text{after}}\,\|\,\pi_{\text{before}}). To avoid data contamination, we use this older model to evaluate against post-release datasets. Further details are available in Appendix B.

Experiment 1: Distribution shift correlates with forgetting across datasets.

[Setup] First, we collect 23 diverse math training datasets, size-matched to 2.5M completion tokens. Datasets are grouped by domain and release date relative to the base model: (1) pre-cutoff, (2) post-cutoff: long chain-of-thought (CoT) math reasoning, and (3) off-target: post-cutoff code or general instruction data.11 1 Although a dataset’s release date does not definitively guarantee whether its tokens were seen during training, it serves as a reasonable proxy for distinguishing between older and newer data. Our overall results and analyses remain robust regardless of this specific grouping. Forgetting is measured as the mean performance drop (Δ\Delta) across five non-math benchmarks: GPQA-Diamond (Rein et al., 2024), ARC-C (Clark et al., 2018), MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024b), HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), and MBPP (Odena et al., 2021). [Results] Fig. 2 (a) demonstrates that the magnitude of forgetting (y-axis) is strongly correlated with the distribution shift of the policy π\pi after fine-tuning (Spearman ρ=−0.85\rho=-0.85), suggesting that updates causing significant distribution shifts are detrimental to continual learning.

Experiment 2: Distribution shift correlates with poor acquisition and forgetting within a dataset.

[Setup] Second, to isolate distribution shift within an underlying dataset, we hold the corpus fixed using OpenR1-Math-220k (Face, 2025), a long-CoT dataset. Using identical prompts, we construct three 2M completion-token datasets that vary only in target text shift: (HI) high shift: full R1 trace with reasoning, (MID) mid shift: R1 final solution without long-CoT, and (LO) low shift: the model’s own verified-correct solution. LO is curated via self-rejection sampling (Singh et al., 2024). The base model decodes a single solution per problem under the same prompt, which is then verified for correctness. [Results] Fig. 2 (c) - (e) show that higher distribution shift tracks with in-domain forgetting and catastrophic forgetting, whereas low-shift self-generated samples improve math acquisition performance while preserving existing coding capabilities.

2.3 Limitations of Self-distillation

Self-supervision fails at small model scales.

Although on-policy self-distillation (SDFT; Shenfeld et al. (2026a)) successfully preserves the base distribution during continual post-training, its efficacy drops for smaller models. Fig. 3(a) demonstrates that SDFT’s performance relative to SFT decreases monotonically with student size. We attribute this to poor self-supervision quality. To evaluate this, we generate an offline dataset to approximate on-policy teacher quality. Fig. 3(b) confirms that smaller models yield weaker supervision: regardless of the prompt (Appendix A), average accuracy falls to 60%, and CoT traces are dropped 8.2% of the time.

2.4 Off-policy In-distribution distillation as Synthetic Self-distillation

To bridge this gap, SynthSelf is designed to (1) remain in-distribution with respect to the base model π\pi, and (2) provide high-quality supervision. We achieve this via two core mechanisms: (i) utilizing off-policy distillation to enable rejection sampling, and (ii) selecting a larger aligner model that simultaneously (ii.a.) yields high-quality supervision, (ii.b.) stays in-distribution relative to the base model, and (ii.c.) incurs low computational overhead.

(i) Off-policy supervision enables rejection sampling.

By generating offline datasets for SFT rather than training on-policy, we can filter for accuracy through rejection sampling. This step is essential because small models are highly sensitive to supervision quality.

(ii) Identifying a low-cost, competent in-distribution aligner.

We formalize the dual objectives of (ii.a.) generating high-quality supervision and (ii.b.) maintaining in-distribution alignment. Let 𝒜={πA(1),…,πA(K)}\mathcal{A}=\{\pi_{A}^{(1)},\dots,\pi_{A}^{(K)}\} be a pool of candidate aligners. We aim to select an aligner πA⋆∈𝒜\pi_{A}^{\star}\in\mathcal{A} that minimizes the distributional gap to the base model, subject to quality constraints (Eq. 6).

Given a demonstration pair (xi,yi)(x_{i},y_{i}) and a rewrite prompt PrewriteP^{\text{rewrite}} (Box A), the aligner’s rewrite distribution is:

qi​(y)≔πA​(y∣Prewrite​(xi,yi)).q_{i}(y)\;\coloneqq\;\pi_{A}\!\left(y\mid P^{\text{rewrite}}(x_{i},y_{i})\right). (2)

This distribution translates the knowledge from (xi,yi)(x_{i},y_{i}) into the aligner’s native distribution. Appendix D shows an example: the rewrite keeps the gold answer and format while restating the reasoning in the aligner’s own phrasing. We decode greedily, y^i,t=arg⁡maxv∈𝒱​πA​(v∣Prewrite​(xi,yi),y^i,<t)\hat{y}_{i,t}=\arg\max_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\,\pi_{A}\!\left(v\mid P^{\text{rewrite}}(x_{i},y_{i}),\,\hat{y}_{i,<t}\right), ensuring a deterministic rewrite y^i\hat{y}_{i}. We measure supervision quality (ii.a.) directly on these rewrites:

R⁡(πA)=𝔼i​[r⁡(xi,y^i)],y^i=greedy⁡(qi),R(\pi_{A})\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{i}\big[r(x_{i},\hat{y}_{i})\big],\qquad\hat{y}_{i}\;=\;\operatorname{greedy}(q_{i}), (3)

where a verifiable reward r(xi,y^i)=𝕀[a(y^i)=a(yi)]r(x_{i},\hat{y}_{i})=\mathbb{I}[a(\hat{y}_{i})=a(y_{i})] checks the extracted answer a⁡(⋅)a(\cdot) against the gold demonstration.

The student is trained to imitate the point mass δy^i\delta_{\hat{y}_{i}} at the mode of qiq_{i}. The divergence against this point mass simplifies to the negative log-likelihood (NLL) under the student π\pi, serving as our metric for in-distribution alignment (ii.b.):

ℒ(πA)=𝔼i[DKL(δy^i∥π(⋅∣xi))]=−𝔼i∑t=1|y^i|logπ(y^i,t∣xi,y^i,<t).\mathcal{L}(\pi_{A})\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{i}\big[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\delta_{\hat{y}_{i}}\,\|\,\pi(\cdot\mid x_{i})\big)\big]\;=\;-\,\mathbb{E}_{i}\sum_{t=1}^{|\hat{y}_{i}|}\log\pi\big(\hat{y}_{i,t}\mid x_{i},\hat{y}_{i,<t}\big). (4)

Standard SFT on gold demonstrations follows an identical objective, replacing δy^i\delta_{\hat{y}_{i}} with δyi\delta_{y_{i}} to provide a baseline divergence:

ℒgold=𝔼i[DKL(δyi∥π(⋅∣xi))]=−𝔼i∑t=1|yi|logπ(yi,t∣xi,yi,<t).\mathcal{L}_{\text{gold}}\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{i}\big[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\delta_{y_{i}}\,\|\,\pi(\cdot\mid x_{i})\big)\big]\;=\;-\,\mathbb{E}_{i}\sum_{t=1}^{|y_{i}|}\log\pi\big(y_{i,t}\mid x_{i},y_{i,<t}\big). (5)

Consequently, we formulate aligner selection as:

πA⋆=arg​minπA∈𝒜⁡ℒ​(πA)s.t.ℒ⁡(πA)​<ℒgoldandR⁡(πA)>​R​(π).\pi_{A}^{\star}\;=\;\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\pi_{A}\in\mathcal{A}}\;\mathcal{L}(\pi_{A})\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad\mathcal{L}(\pi_{A})\;<\;\mathcal{L}_{\text{gold}}\quad\text{and}\quad R(\pi_{A})\;>\;R(\pi). (6)

In short, we select the aligner closest in distribution to the student. The constraints guarantee its rewrites offer a distributional advantage over standard SFT (ℒ⁡(πA)<ℒgold\mathcal{L}(\pi_{A})<\mathcal{L}_{\text{gold}}) and strictly exceed the base model’s supervision quality (R⁡(πA)>R⁡(π)R(\pi_{A})>R(\pi)).

In practice, scaling up within the same model family perfectly satisfies Eq. 6. Fig. 5 shows that same-family aligners (Qwen2.5-7B, 14B, 32B) achieve the lowest average KL, falling well below ℒgold\mathcal{L}_{\text{gold}}, whereas stronger cross-family models fail to meaningfully reduce the NLL (averaged across three domains detailed in § 3). Furthermore, same-family aligners yield higher data accuracy than the base model, satisfying R⁡(πA)>R⁡(π)R(\pi_{A})>R(\pi) (Tab. 2). Finally, to satisfy the low-cost constraint (ii.c.), we instantiate πA⋆\pi_{A}^{\star} using minimally larger Qwen2.5-7B and 14B models, ensuring minimal computational overhead.

Algorithmic implementation.

Using this minimally larger same-family aligner πA\pi_{A}, we implement SynthSelf (see Alg. 1). We first initialize an empty offline dataset 𝒟^\hat{\mathcal{D}} (Line 1). Next, processing the data in batches, we generate an in-distribution rewrite y^i\hat{y}_{i} for each sample ii via the aligner πA\pi_{A} using greedy decoding (Lines 2 and 3). Samples that satisfy the rejection sampling are then added to 𝒟^\hat{\mathcal{D}} (Lines 4 to 8). Finally, we perform SFT on this filtered dataset 𝒟^\hat{\mathcal{D}} to update the base model parameters (Line 10).

3 Empirical Study

We evaluate SynthSelf on the three domains from SDFT (Shenfeld et al., 2026a), alongside a 4-subject science mixture to verify generalization. In §3.3, we further analyze our approach by: (i) demonstrating that distribution matching outweighs aligner capability; (ii) benchmarking against SDFT on matched and diverse prompts; and (iii) ablating rejection sampling to confirm the value of off-policy supervision.

3.1 Experimental Protocol

Baselines.

We compare our method against four baselines: standard SFT, SDFT (Shenfeld et al., 2026a), DFT (Wu et al., 2026), which modifies the objective function to imitate on-policy learning, naturally inducing in-distribution learning, and ASFT (Zhu et al., 2026), which improves upon DFT by further mitigating distributional shift. To control for the larger aligner model size, we also compare SynthSelf against off- and on-policy distillation (Agarwal et al., 2024). Here, off-policy distillation is equivalent to Alg. 1, but conditions the generation on the original query xix_{i} rather than the rewrite prompt Prewrite​(xi,yi)P^{\text{rewrite}}(x_{i},y_{i}). We tune standard SFT minimally and fix these hyperparameters across all methods for fairness. To ensure a strong baseline, we additionally optimize SDFT’s skip-token hyperparameter; which discards TT initial formatting tokens. Conversely, SynthSelf is tuning-free and introduces zero additional hyperparameters.

Datasets and models.

Following Shenfeld et al. (2026a), we evaluate on three domains: science (SciKnowEval Chemistry L-3; Feng et al. (2025)), tool-use (ToolAlpaca; Tang et al. (2023)), and medicine (MedMCQA; Pal et al. (2022)). We expand to all four SciKnowEval subjects for our mixture experiment. We substitute the medical dataset used by Shenfeld et al. (2026a) with MedMCQA to avoid LLM-as-a-judge evaluation and improve reproducibility. We adopt the Qwen2.5-Instruct family as base models, unlike later versions like Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025) exhaustively trained on open-source data; this choice reduces contamination and ensures demonstration novelty. Further experimental details are in Appendix C.

3.2 Results

SynthSelf achieves the highest acquisition across all four benchmarks, including the science mixture, while matching the strongest baselines on 14 retention tasks (Tab. 1, Fig. 1). We abbreviate SynthSelf as SS, with 1Δ\Delta and 2Δ\Delta denoting aligners one and two sizes larger, respectively (i.e., Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B). Interestingly, recent methods fail to surpass SFT in acquisition at these smaller scales. DFT’s performance in the medical domain deteriorates especially significantly; we have double-checked that these evaluation values are correct. However, consistent with the discussion in § 2.2.1, the on-policy and in-distribution mechanisms of SDFT and ASFT successfully improve retention over SFT.

Moreover, we validate that the performance gains of SynthSelf stem primarily from in-distribution demonstration injection, rather than merely leveraging a larger aligner (Tab. 1). Off- and on-policy distillation (Off-/On-PD) use the identical aligner, differing only in conditioning on xix_{i} rather than on Prewrite​(xi,yi)P^{\text{rewrite}}(x_{i},y_{i}). Averaged across all four settings, SynthSelf nonetheless improves acquisition by +5.7%p to +16.9%p while maintaining comparable retention. As expected, demonstration injection drives these acquisition gains, whereas all three methods (SynthSelf, Off-PD, and On-PD) similarly preserve the base model distribution to sustain retention capabilities. Lastly, we observe that SynthSelf does not yield significant improvements over Off-/On-PD in the medical domain. This is likely due to the aligner models already having perfect knowledge of the training data, making demonstration injection largely redundant. Despite this, SynthSelf remains highly competitive, successfully outperforming all remaining baselines.

3.3 Further Experimental Analyses

Distribution matching outweighs aligner capability, and leads to data generation cost savings.

We validate our hypothesis that lower-cost, in-distribution aligners are more effective than stronger out-of-distribution (OOD) alternatives. Although larger aligners like Qwen3.5-27B and Gemma-4-31B (Team et al., 2026) generate higher-quality supervision (measured via data-generation accuracy), they introduce severe distributional shift relative to the base model. Consequently, they yield similar or worse acquisition performance (Tab. 2). Moreover, using a same-family aligner reduces data generation inference costs by 62.9% to 76.9% FLOPs.

SynthSelf outperforms prompt-matched self-distillation.

We confirm that SynthSelf’s gains over SDFT do not arise from differences in supervision prompts (Fig. 6). Evaluating four SDFT prompt variants, including one matched to SynthSelf, we find our method consistently achieves higher acquisition across all three domains and higher average retention than every variant. Full prompts are provided in Appendix A.

Rejection sampling ablation.

Finally, we ablate the offline data generation that enables rejection sampling (Alg. 1, Lines 4–7). As shown in Fig. 5, this filtering mechanism consistently improves both SynthSelf and Off-PD. We hypothesize such filtering is especially critical for smaller base models, which are highly sensitive to noisy supervision.

4 Discussion

Additional related work.

Huang et al. (2026) highlights the impact of distribution drift in SFT using code-generation data on Qwen3-8B. However, they do not directly address continual learning or small language models, restricting their evaluation to limited scales and domains. Furthermore, Li et al. (2026) combines mechanisms that we instead isolate: SDFT-style self-rewrites with similarity filtering, cross-family fusion, and an on-policy KL regularizer; covered individually by our SDFT, on-policy distillation, and ASFT baselines. Crucially, we differ in the supervision source. Because their rewrites originate from the student, they inherit the small-scale degradation shown in Fig. 3. Our same-family aligner explicitly resolves this limitation.

Training compute savings and further performance headroom.

Rejection sampling reduces training compute by shrinking the dataset |D^||\hat{D}| (e.g., by 17.1% for tool use; Tab. 2). Despite training on fewer demonstrations than SFT, SynthSelf improves acquisition by +4.2%p on average, proving these gains stem from supervision quality rather than quantity. To further boost performance, practitioners can scale kk in pass@kk, trading inference compute for larger coverage supervision.

Limitation and future directions.

SynthSelf requires a larger, same-family aligner. Fortunately, most major open-weight families provide a spectrum of model sizes, naturally satisfying this requirement since smaller variants are often distilled from their larger counterparts (e.g., Qwen2.5, Qwen3.5, OLMo 2 (Walsh et al., 2025), Llama 3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024), and Gemma 4). Nevertheless, future work could explore adapting out-of-family aligners to produce in-distribution supervision. One promising direction is adding the base model’s answer in-context with an appropriate prompt to generate an in-distribution rewrite.

AI use statement

We used generative AI to assist with experimental code generation and reviewing writing for grammar and spelling. Furthermore, language models generated the reasoning demonstrations for three SciKnowEval subjects. The Chemistry demonstrations were generated with GPT-4o by Shenfeld et al. (2026a). AI was not used for conceptualization, methodology design, data analysis, or result interpretation. All reported numbers were produced directly by our experimental pipeline, not by a language model. The authors reviewed all AI-assisted scripts and text, and we take full responsibility for the final content of this work.

Appendix

Appendix A Prompts

Prompt A is PrewriteP^{\text{rewrite}}, the instruction behind every trained SynthSelf cell. Prompts B, C and D are the rewrite variants used in the self-rewrite study (§ 2.2.1) and the prompt-matched SDFT ablation (§ 3.3). {q} and {gold} are the question and the gold response.

Appendix B Setup for the In-distribution Experiments

Both experiments continue fine-tuning Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct in bf16 with LoRA (r=16r{=}16, α=32\alpha{=}32, all linear layers) for 11 epoch at a constant learning rate of 10−410^{-4} with AdamW, seed 11, and differ only in the training data. Decoding is greedy. Tab. 3 lists every dataset Experiment 1 trains on, with its source and upload date.

Appendix C Further Experimental Details

C.1 Hardware

All experiments run on A100 nodes. For other hardware such as CPU, RAM and disk we use commonly available ones, as these did not induce any bottlenecks.

C.2 Datasets

All datasets are set to default values following the SDFT paper. Tab. 4 gives the Science Mixture split. SciKnowEval supplies only an answer key for its multiple-choice rows, so the <reasoning> demonstrations every arm trains on or rewrites are model-generated: GPT-4o for Chemistry, released by Shenfeld et al. (2026a), and gpt-5.6-luna for the other three subjects. Gold is therefore the subset of the L-3 pool a correct demonstration exists for, split 8080/2020 into training and test, so the evaluation prompts are filtered the same way, though every arm is scored on the same pool.

C.3 Training Configuration

Tab. 5 lists the settings. Every cell is a single seed 4242 chosen a priori, and never changed after experimentation.
